extracted.intended_audience: journalists and other communications professionals (reporters, editors, media writers)
extracted.subtask_description: A journalism-focused style guide offering term-by-term recommendations and general principles for how to refer to people with disabilities in reporting, including when to mention disabilities, phrasing preferences (person-first vs identity-first), and AP-style alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to a disability only when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to a disability only when it’s relevant to the story and, when possible, confirm the diagnosis with a reputable source, such as a medical professional or other licensed professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: omit a wheelchair user's disability when it doesn't affect the story (e.g., airplane noise complaint); include blindness when it contributed to being stranded. When in doubt, omit. Confirm diagnoses before reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask sources how they would like to be described
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, ask sources how they would like to be described. If the source is not available or unable to communicate, ask a trusted family member, advocate, medical professional or relevant organization that represents people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect individual preferences; no single default applies to everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid made-up euphemisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid made-up words like “diversability” and “handicapable” unless using them in direct quotes or to refer to a movement or organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard, widely understood terms rather than neologisms except when clearly contextualized or quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with terms that imply judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sensitive when using words like “disorder,” “impairment,” “abnormality” and “special” to describe the nature of a disability. The word “condition” is often a good substitute that avoids judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize there is no universal agreement on these terms; some contexts (medical, legal, program names) may warrant use. Prefer neutral phrasing when possible (e.g., 'condition').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid value-laden functional labels (high/low functioning, severe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid labels such as “high functioning” and “low functioning” because they are considered offensive; prefer terms like “significant” rather than “severe” when appropriate and proceed with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing level of function, be specific about abilities or impacts rather than relying on vague evaluative phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use derogatory terms in quotes only when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: You may end up using a derogatory term in a direct quote, but be certain that it’s fundamental to the story. Otherwise, paraphrase and use a more acceptable term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous repetition of slurs; contextualize and minimize harm while preserving accuracy when quotes are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal default on person-first vs identity-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide no longer prescribes a default (person-first vs identity-first); instead, reporters should ask individuals how they prefer to be described and confirm on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific guidance in individual term entries; when interviewing, prioritize the source’s stated preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guide when you cannot ask the person
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot ask the person how they want to be described, use this guide as a resource and do your best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide provides term-specific recommendations to follow in absence of a stated preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider context and audience for evolving terms (COVID-19 example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language around emerging conditions (e.g., 'long COVID') is evolving; reporters should consult well-considered sources and be attentive to changing preferences and terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite reputable sources when adopting newer terms; be explicit when a term is new or contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Able-bodied
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid implying that all people with disabilities lack 'able bodies' — some prefer 'non-disabled' or 'enabled' as more accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ recommends 'non-disabled' or phrases like 'does not have a disability' as more neutral choices; 'able-bodied' can be appropriate in some contexts (e.g., government reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ableism/Ableist
rubrics_metrics.description: Ableism refers to discrimination and social prejudice against people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term but explain it for mainstream audiences; be cautious about labeling individuals as 'ableist' without context (similar caution to calling someone racist/sexist). The AP has updated definitions aligning ableism with other -isms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abnormal/abnormality
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'abnormal'/'abnormality' to describe people as it is derogatory; acceptable in medical/scientific contexts to describe phenomena or test results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'typical' when comparing to non-disabled people; explain context when using 'abnormal behavior.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Addict/addiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use people-first phrasing for addiction (e.g., 'someone with a drug addiction'); avoid derogatory terms like 'junkie.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow public-health guidance: don't use 'clean'/'dirty' for drug tests (say 'tested positive'); prefer 'misuse' over 'abuse'; distinguish 'dependence' from 'addiction'; use 'recovering' or 'in recovery' when appropriate; conforms to AP guidance on phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afflicted with/stricken with/suffers from/victim of
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid terms that assume suffering or victimhood; they connote pity and can be inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral language: state the condition (e.g., 'He has muscular dystrophy'). Conforms to AP advice to avoid pity-laden descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Albino/albinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Many prefer the people-first term 'person with albinism' because 'albino' has been used hatefully in history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to a person with albinism rather than calling someone 'an albino'; be aware debate over whether albinism is a disability (often referred to as such due to vision issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcoholic/alcoholism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use people-first language for alcoholism (e.g., 'a person with alcoholism' or 'a person with an alcohol addiction') rather than labeling someone an 'alcoholic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'recovering' for those in recovery; conform to AP guidance to avoid terms like 'alcoholic' unless preferred by the individual or in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcoholics Anonymous membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Because anonymity is central to AA, disclose membership only if essential to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering AA, consider referring to members by first name only unless context requires otherwise; same care applies to other 12-step programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the full name on first reference; ADA acceptable thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Sign Language (ASL)/signer/interpreter
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify 'American Sign Language' on first reference (capitalize all three words); ASL acceptable on second reference. Use 'interpreter' only for those with advanced training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate 'signer' (conversational ability) from 'interpreter' (professionally trained); consult Registry of Interpreters of the Deaf for registered interpreters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amputation/amputee
rubrics_metrics.description: Use people-first phrasing like 'someone with an amputation' rather than potentially offensive labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'amputee' may be offensive to some; ask preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asperger’s/Asperger’s syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Asperger's was folded into autism spectrum disorder (DSM-5), avoid using 'Asperger’s' and instead refer to autism/autism spectrum disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ASAN recommendation: refer to autism or autism spectrum disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to ADHD only if relevant and if you are confident there is a medical diagnosis; use full name on first reference, ADHD thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask sources whether they prefer 'have' or 'are' ADHD; if uncertain, ask and follow preference. AP style: not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the term 'audism' (oppression/judgment of deaf people based on hearing norms) but explain it for mainstream audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is accepted but may need definition for readers unfamiliar with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the full phrase on first reference and explain what it means; AAC acceptable on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible when interviewing non-speaking sources; try alternate communication methods if one fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autism/autism spectrum disorder/autistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to autism only if relevant and if confident of a medical diagnosis; ask how individuals prefer to be described (some prefer 'autistic' identity-first).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP accepts 'autism' as umbrella term; people's preferences vary widely — confirm case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipolar disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to someone as having bipolar disorder only if relevant and diagnosed; if diagnosis is unconfirmed, use quotes and state that it is unconfirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'bipolar' as a colloquial adjective for non-medical phenomena; AP style cautions against casual use of mental health terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind/legally blind/low vision/visually impaired
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'blind' for complete or almost complete loss of sight; use terms like 'low vision' or 'limited vision' for partial loss; ask people what they prefer, including identity-first vs person-first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because terms are imprecise, consider asking how the visual condition affects acuity; follow preferences; AP suggests 'visually impaired' or 'person with low vision' for some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain injury/traumatic brain injury (TBI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'person with a brain injury' or 'person with a traumatic brain injury' rather than derogatory terms like 'brain damaged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow medical definitions (CDC) and avoid casual/pejorative language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caregiver vs caretaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'caregiver' when referring to people who provide direct care to individuals; 'caretaker' implies caring for property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catatonia/catatonic
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to someone as 'catatonic' only if it is part of a medical diagnosis; avoid casual use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'catatonic' informally can be offensive and inaccurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cerebral palsy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to describe a person as 'someone with cerebral palsy' and to provide a brief explanation of the condition when relevant; avoid using 'spastic' as an insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing symptoms, ask the person what terms they prefer; note that 'spastic' or 'a spaz' are derogatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical and/or electrical sensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'person with chemical intolerance' or 'people with environmental illness' rather than derogatory labels like 'chemophobic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions may be described as 'toxicant-induced loss of tolerance' or 'sick-building syndrome' in some literature; provide definitions as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronic disease/chronic illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Only refer to a chronic illness if pertinent to the story and if you are confident there is a medical diagnosis; ask how people want to be described (some prefer 'person with diabetes' rather than 'a diabetic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about equating chronic illness with disability — debate exists; AP style not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleft palate or lip/harelip
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'person who has a cleft palate' and avoid using the term 'harelip' as it is anatomically incorrect and stigmatizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochlear implant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid describing cochlear implants as corrective devices that 'restore' hearing or as a means to return someone to 'mainstream' society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the device as an electronic aid that can assist some people who are deaf or hard of hearing in understanding speech; be aware of cultural concerns within the Deaf community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorblind
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'colorblind' is still generally acceptable, but 'color vision deficiency' is more accurate and less ableist; consider specifying the type (e.g., red-green).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using 'color vision deficiency,' be prepared to explain its meaning to general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congenital disability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to state that someone has a congenital disability or 'has had a disability since birth'; be specific about the condition when possible and avoid the term 'defect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'defect' or 'defective' because they imply inferiority; AP recommends specifying the condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crazy/loony/mad/psycho/nuts/deranged
rubrics_metrics.description: These words are offensive when used to describe mental illness and should be avoided except in essential quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use these words, particularly when reporting on mental illness, unless they are part of an essential quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cretin/cretinism
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'cretin' is considered a slur for people with intellectual disabilities; use clinical terms such as 'hypothyroidism' instead where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pejorative historical terms; choose accurate medical diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripple/crip
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'cripple' as noun or verb to describe people unless referring to the reclaimed 'crip' movement or quoting; many find it offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the term is used by activists in reclaimed contexts, explain and limit usage; otherwise avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cued speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'cued speech' is not commonly used in the U.S., include a definition when using the term and note that it is not interchangeable with ASL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that it is a system of hand signs and spots near the mouth to differentiate sounds and is not sign language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'deaf' or 'hard of hearing' depending on audiological status and individual preference; capitalize 'Deaf' when referring to the cultural community and use lowercase when referring to the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'hearing impaired' unless the person uses it; ask about identity-first vs person-first preferences. When reporting signed responses, indicate that responses were signed on first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf-blind/deafblind/DeafBlind
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms deaf-blind, deafblind and deaf-blindness are all acceptable; ask individuals which term they prefer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some organizations use hyphenation while others prefer concatenated forms; respect individual and organizational preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf and dumb/deaf-mute
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid these terms because they inaccurately imply inability to communicate and have offensive connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'deaf' or 'hard of hearing' and be specific about communication methods (ASL, lip-reading, writing) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect/birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'defect' or 'defective' to describe a person’s disability; use specific condition names and only use 'birth defect' in broad references or when appropriate in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP allows 'birth defect' in broad references but not when referring to a specific person or group; consider 'congenital disorder' if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformed/deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'deformed' or 'deformity' to describe people in a stigmatizing way; when discussing physical differences, be specific and sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clinical or descriptive language rather than pejorative terms; explain medically when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychotic/psychosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'psychotic' and 'psychosis' only when they accurately describe a medical experience; avoid using 'psychotic' as a general adjective for people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer phrasing such as 'having a psychotic condition' or 'experiencing a psychosis' rather than labeling a person as psychotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadriplegia/quadriplegic (tetraplegia/tetraplegic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask people how they want to be described; many prefer people-first language ('a person with quadriplegia') rather than identity-labeling adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some people use reclaimed terms or shortened forms ('quads') — use in quotes if the person self-identifies that way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retarded / Mentally retarded
rubrics_metrics.description: See entry on 'Mentally Retarded' — historically used clinical terms are now slurs and should be avoided; use contemporary, non-stigmatizing clinical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with appropriate, person-first clinical terminology and avoid derogatory usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schizophrenia/schizophrenic
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to someone as having schizophrenia only if relevant and diagnosed; prefer 'a person with schizophrenia' rather than 'a schizophrenic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If diagnosis is unconfirmed, use quotes and indicate uncertainty. Do not use 'schizophrenic' colloquially to describe non-health issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not say someone has had a seizure unless there has been a medical diagnosis; if medical diagnosis is unconfirmed, use quotes and indicate that a diagnosis has not been confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a person who had a seizure has epilepsy; provide medical context where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service animal/assistance animal/guide dog
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'service animal,' 'assistance animal,' and 'guide dog' are acceptable; avoid using 'Seeing Eye dog' (trademark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the federal ADA definition for scope; be aware that licensure/certification issues are contentious in the disability community — prefer the federal definition when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short stature (dwarf/little person/midget)
rubrics_metrics.description: See dedicated entry on dwarf/short stature; generally avoid slurs and follow individual preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use respectful, specific terminology and ask individuals for their preferred terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/special needs/functional needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'special' or 'special needs' to describe people; be specific about disabilities or use 'functional needs' when referring to accessibility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use program or organization formal names only when required; avoid shorthand acronyms like 'SPED' which are offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech impediment/Speech disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using 'speech disability' instead of 'speech impediment,' 'disorder' or 'impairment' which can sound deficit-focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, use neutral or person-first language and ask about preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spina bifida
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to describe a person as 'someone with spina bifida' and provide a brief explanation of the condition if pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about type and impacts when relevant to the story; AP style not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stuttering/stammering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'stuttering' rather than 'stammering'; people-first language ('a person who stutters') is generally preferred though some prefer 'stutterer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the clinical 'childhood-onset fluency disorder' without explanation; ask about preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffers from/victim of/afflicted with (reiteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pity-framing language such as 'suffers from' or 'victim of' when describing disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral factual phrasing; refrain from framing disability as an affliction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide reporting language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sensationalizing language; avoid 'committed suicide' except in direct quotations and use alternatives such as 'died by suicide' or 'took her own life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'unsuccessful suicide attempt' — use 'attempted suicide.' Distinguish euthanasia/medically assisted suicide terminology carefully and follow AP guidance and resources like reportingonsuicide.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivor/battle metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that 'survivor' and 'battle' metaphors (e.g., 'cancer survivor'/'battle cancer') may offend some; they are still widely used but should be applied with sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms like 'survivor' with care due to imprecision and potential to offend; consider the individual’s preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tetraplegia/tetraplegic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use people-first language like 'a person with tetraplegia' rather than labeling someone as 'tetraplegic' unless the person prefers the adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar guidance as quadriplegia; ask sources about preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers/Content warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alerting audiences (or students) ahead of time if content contains graphic descriptions of traumatic events that may trigger psychological reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger warnings can build audience trust; avoid using the phrase flippantly. AP suggests content warnings at top of stories when material may be offensive or disturbing but not when profanity is the only concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tourette syndrome/Tourette’s
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Tourette syndrome' without a possessive or capitalization of 'syndrome'; refer to someone as 'having Tourette syndrome' only if relevant and medically diagnosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many prefer people-first language; avoid acronym TS as it is not widely known; AP defines the condition but offers no further stylistic prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/treatment center/rehab center/detox center
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'treatment' for medical interventions and 'treatment center' instead of 'rehab' or 'detox' center; refer to someone enrolled as a 'patient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow medical-community definitions; avoid slang terms that can be stigmatizing.
